subject: Critical Thinking
title: Rhetorical Tricks: Loaded Questions and False Dilemmas
description: A short lesson to help you apply Rhetorical Tricks: Loaded Questions and False Dilemmas.

hook.text: 'Have you stopped cheating on tests?' Yes or no, you're guilty. That's a loaded question — it presupposes guilt.

buildup.text: Loaded questions embed false assumptions. False dilemmas present only two options when more exist.

discovery.text: 'You're either with us or against us' – a false dilemma.

punchline.text: When someone limits your options, they're controlling the conversation.

quiz.question: What is a loaded question?
options: A question that contains a false or unproven assumption
A question with too many parts

details.summary: Rhetorical tricks like loaded questions and false dilemmas manipulate debates by constraining how you can answer. Recognizing these tactics lets you refuse the rigged setup and reframe the conversation.
details.whyItMatters: If you accept a loaded question's premise or a false dilemma's limited options, you have already lost the argument before you begin.
takeaways: False dilemmas present only two options when more exist
Refusing the trick's framing is the correct response

faq.question: What is an example of a loaded question in everyday conversation?
faq.answer: Asking 'Have you stopped wasting company time?' assumes you were wasting it. Any yes-or-no answer accepts the hidden premise. The correct move is to challenge the assumption directly.

faq.question: How do you respond when someone presents a false dilemma?
faq.answer: Point out the missing options. If someone says 'You're either with us or against us,' note that neutral, partially supportive, and conditional positions also exist. Breaking the binary reframes the debate.
